answers.U2-S1: Nature prepares for the next season well before the current one ends; new buds and growth form in late summer and fall, ready for spring.
answers.U2-S2: To correct a popular but inaccurate idea: he uses it as a starting point to explain that new buds form in the leaf axil long before leaves fall.
answers.U2-S3: A playful, humorous personification, attributing a human character flaw (indecisiveness, slovenliness) to trees that keep their dead leaves.
answers.U2-S4: Dropping old leaves is an active process needing a healthy tree; a weak or suddenly killed tree keeps its withered leaves, so letting go shows vigor.
answers.U2-S5: Beginning or origin; the start of the next season's growth.
answers.U2-S6: He partly agrees that growth starts before spring but says the real start is even earlier, in late summer, when trees form new buds.
answers.U2-S7: Both hold fully formed future life, packed and protected, waiting for spring warmth to 'hatch' them; like insect eggs laid in late summer, they look ahead.
answers.U2-S8: Each season produces and prepares the beginnings of the following one; next year's growth originates within the current year.
answers.U2-S9: His own direct observation of nature: examining fallen leaves, cutting open buds, watching specific trees and plants.
answers.U2-S10: It sums up and restates the passage's main idea with a household metaphor: nature always prepares for spring before winter arrives.
